# Set up an agent operating model

Generate a project's agent operating model: a main session acting as CEO, leads per area, specialists, a fixed report format, per-task model and effort rules with a floor in every agent file, a review cadence, and per-area practices for how agents work on each kind of thing. Read, ask little, propose once, write after one "yes".

## Step 1 — Read the project

Collect signals and record the path each came from. The list and how to count areas are in [references/sizing-signals.md](references/sizing-signals.md). Count code volume with a command that prints totals (`find … | wc -l` style), never by reading files. Read, when present: `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/PRD.md`, `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/CONVENTIONS.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, and the user's `CLAUDE.md` if it is reachable.

If `.claude/agents/` or an `OPERATING-MODEL.md` already exists, switch to update mode: follow [references/update-mode.md](references/update-mode.md) for every later step.

Count recent commits (for example `git log --since="8 weeks ago" --oneline`) to set the periodic review's frequency: weekly at 8 or more commits in that window, every two weeks at 3–7, monthly at 2 or fewer.

From the `CLAUDE.md` files, note what the environment already decides and inherit it instead of inventing it:

- **Language.** The owner's language sets the language of reports, questions and headings, and the agent file names: Portuguese → `lider-<area>.md` / `especialista-<tarefa>.md`; any other → `lead-<area>.md` / `specialist-<task>.md`.
- **Shell and context tooling rules.** If a `CLAUDE.md` already has rules for shell commands or for reading files, the protocol points at them; never copy them. If none exist, write nothing about it.
- **Owner working style.** Use the environment's own and never override it. Offer the items of [references/owner-working-style.md](references/owner-working-style.md) that it does not settle in Step 4, each off until the owner turns it on.

## Step 2 — Size the model

Count justified areas and pick the tier from the table in [references/sizing-signals.md](references/sizing-signals.md): Small (1–2, no leads), Medium (3–5), Large (6+). Code volume only breaks a tie at a boundary. Every area and every agent must trace to a signal; drop anything that doesn't. **Each lead owns exactly one area and each specialist does one kind of work:** never merge areas into one lead or kinds of work into one specialist. An area the owner names in answer to question 2 counts, with ``Signal: `owner answer, question 2` `` (or its ROADMAP path).

Map the justified areas to their practices files (`docs/practices/<area>.md`: how agents work on screens, APIs, deploys, security, legal texts, marketing, product) with the table in [references/practices.md](references/practices.md).

## Step 3 — Ask at most three questions

Only what the repo cannot show, one question per message, multiple choice, your inferred answer first as the recommendation. **Skip any question the request already answers**; if all three are answered, go straight to the proposal.

1. Who the human owner is: one person or a team.
2. Areas planned that have no code yet.
3. What must never happen without the owner (extends the owner-only list).

Every other open point goes into the proposal as an editable default — never a fourth question.

## Step 4 — Propose, in one message

Use this shape so it can be checked line by line, in the owner's language for prose but with these literal keys:

```
Tier: <Small|Medium|Large> (<N> justified areas)
Chain of command: owner → main session → <leads → >specialists

Areas
- <area> — <one line>. Signal: `<path>`

Agents
- <file name> (<lead|specialist|reviewer>, model <alias> / effort <level>) — <one line>. Signal: `<path>`

Editable defaults
- Worktrees: read-only work only (change if your tooling allows agents to commit there)
- Periodic agent review: off until you say yes; <weekly | from commit rhythm> when on
- Security posture: <pre-launch (guards only for production, real users' data, money or a hard constraint) | in production | off>
- Owner working style (items the environment does not settle), each off until you turn it on: <numbered item names from references/owner-working-style.md>
- Area practice options, each off until you turn it on: <the options of the proposed practices files, one line each>
- <other defaults>

Files
- create docs/OPERATING-MODEL.md
- create docs/practices/<area>.md  (one line per practices file)
- create .claude/agents/<name>.md  (one line per agent)
- create|change CLAUDE.md — adds the "Operating model" pointer section
```

For a `CLAUDE.md` that already exists, show the section's diff right after the block; that diff is its per-file approval, so the one "yes" covers it. Small tier lists no lead. Floors come from [references/model-effort.md](references/model-effort.md). Then stop and wait. Write nothing before an explicit yes.

## Step 5 — Write, after one "yes"

- `docs/OPERATING-MODEL.md` from [templates/operating-model.md](templates/operating-model.md); drop the lead layer and its sections for Small tier, and fill the security posture and owner working style parts from the approved defaults.
- One `docs/practices/<area>.md` per approved practices file, from [templates/practices/](templates/practices/), keeping only the options turned on ([references/practices.md](references/practices.md) § Writing them).
- One `.claude/agents/` file per approved agent, from [templates/lead.md](templates/lead.md) or [templates/specialist.md](templates/specialist.md), each listing its area's practices files under **Read first**. Every `description` is one line of at most about 160 characters, since the Agent tool lists every description on every turn. Every file sets its `model` and `effort` floor. 1	# Owner working style
2	
3	The way one owner wants to be worked with, offered as a pack of items for any owner to pick from. Each item is off until the owner turns it on in the proposal. Skip an item the environment's `CLAUDE.md` files already settle; never override them. The items turned on are written into `docs/OPERATING-MODEL.md` § Talking to the owner, worded for the project.
4	
5	## Asking
6	
7	1. **One decision per question.** 2–4 options with the recommended one first; a question about a visual detail comes with the images.
8	2. **No question that changes nothing.** A notice (such as "merge now?") is not a question; ask only when the answer changes what happens next.
9	3. **Answer "why" with the fault.** An answer to the owner's "why…" starts with what was wrong in the action.
10	4. **Summary before approval.** Before asking to approve a PRD, spec or plan, a short summary in the owner's language: what gets built and what doesn't, the owner's own steps and when, costs, decisions made without the owner, the main risks and what stays unverified.
11	
12	## The owner's steps
13	
14	5. **Fewer manual tasks.** Before writing "the owner does X", check whether an agent can do it. What stays with the owner is only what agents must not do (security settings, merges into the default branch, credentials, money). The rest goes in one short batch at the end, with the page already open and how long it takes. A refusal is said once.
15	6. **Step lists.** Two headed lists, the owner's and the agents', each step marked now or later. A task reaches the owner only validated, in one list. Each step that involves a sign-in names the exact account, where any code comes from, and to sign out of the owner's own account first. Commands are one plain copy-paste block, no shell functions. Logins are grouped into one sitting per day.
16	7. **Third-party signups.** A recommendation to create an account on a service carries the exact signup URL, each choice on each screen, and the options that lead somewhere paid or irreversible, from the current flow, researched.
17	8. **Manual tests.** Agents start every process a manual test needs and check that each is ready before the owner opens the browser, and stop them after. The way one owner wants to be worked with, offered as a pack of items for any owner to pick from. Each item is off until the owner turns it on in the proposal. 1. **One decision per question.** 2–4 options with the recommended one first; a question about a visual detail comes with the images.
2. **No question that changes nothing.** A notice (such as "merge now?") is not a question; ask only when the answer changes what happens next.
3. **Answer "why" with the fault.** An answer to the owner's "why…" starts with what was wrong in the action.

5. **Fewer manual tasks.** Before writing "the owner does X", check whether an agent can do it. 30	| {{area}} | `{{lead}}` | `{{specialist}}`, … | `{{path}}` |
31

33	
34	## Models and effort
35	
36	Every spawn sets `model` explicitly, and sets `effort` explicitly where the CLI supports the per-invocation parameter (Claude Code 2.1.292 or later). Otherwise the floor in the agent file applies. Models are named by alias, never by full ID.
37	
38	| Work | `model` | `effort` |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| Lookups and formatting | `sonnet` (or `haiku`, see below) | `low` |
41	| Mechanical work: routine edits, docs, config, ports a plan already defines — and its review | `sonnet` for the work, `opus` for the review | `medium` |
42	| Real logic, design | `opus` | `high` for logic; `medium` when a plan already holds the design |
43	| Fixes of review findings | as for the work | `medium` |
44	| Review where production personal data, money, auth or a hard constraint is at stake | `opus` | `high` |
45	| Leads | `opus` | `medium`, `high` for a hard area |
46	| Anything at `xhigh` or `max` | — | Only with the main session's explicit OK |
47	
48	- `haiku` with `low` only for a lookup whose answer can be checked, or for running a gate and summarizing its result. Never for logic, security, personal data, money, docs, reviews or leads. Its output is checked by a script or by its spawner before use; a lookup a script can answer needs no agent.
49	- Each agent file carries a floor (`model`/`effort` in its frontmatter) for spawns that omit the parameters. The floor is a safety net, not the choice.
50	- Prefer resuming a finished agent with `SendMessage` over spawning a new one for the same thread of work.
51	- The main session delegates every research, extraction, measurement and analysis from the first step; it briefs, decides and checks. Its effort is never lowered to save tokens.
52	- **Titles.** The Agent tool's `description` is the title the owner sees in the agent list. It starts with who the agent is, a pipe, then the task: `<Role> | <task>` (an ad-hoc member: `<Area> › <role> | <task>`). A title can't change later and a resumed agent keeps it, so a lead is named for its role, not its first task. Leads title their own spawns the same way.
53	- **Waiting for children.** A lead waits for every child it spawned to return, and hands back with their work committed. A child resumed with `SendMessage` runs in the background, even when its first run was in the foreground: a lead that resumes a child and needs its result does not end its turn, and waits with one blocking command that ends on the child's commit or report, never with repeated calls. If the lead is told to hand back while a child still runs, its report's status line is `BLOCKED: waiting for <child id>`, and the main session resumes the lead only after that child's notification.
54	- Before integrating a lead's work into a shared checkout, the main session runs `git status`; uncommitted work there means it resumes the lead to finish it.
55	- **Lead rotation:** a lead is replaced by a fresh one at each plan stop point, or when its transcript passes about {{5 MB}} of text (images excluded) or {{150}} model turns, whichever comes first. It is measured at each hand-back and before each `SendMessage` resume. (default — tune)
56	
57	## Talking to the owner
58	
59	- Only the main session talks to the owner. {{Point at the owner-contact rules already in CLAUDE.md, if any; then list here the owner working style items the owner turned on.}}
60	- Before asking, the main session checks whether the docs already answer the question; if so, it answers itself and cites the file.
61	- A prompt meant for an outside tool (a paid generator, an external service) is shown to the owner and approved before it is sent; a change of wording goes back to the owner.
62	- Subagents cannot ask the owner. When they need a decision they stop at a safe point and end their report with a questions block. The main session asks the owner, then resumes the agent with `SendMessage`, passing the answers verbatim.
63	- Before acting in a browser where the owner is signed in, the main session says in one line the site, the element and the text it will type, and acts on the owner's yes.
64	
65	### Report format (every agent)
66	
67	Headings in {{language}}. The first line is the status, so the spawner can act on it before reading the rest:
68	
69	```
70	<DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED: <reason> | <reviewer verdict>>
71	## Report — <agent> — <task>
72	**Result:** <one line>
73	**Done:** <bullets>
74	**Evidence:** <commands run and what they returned, files>
75	**Files and commits:** <paths, commit hashes>
76	**Questions:**
77	1. <question> — context: <one line>; options: A (recommended) …, B …; blocking: yes/no; meanwhile: <what was done or skipped while waiting>
78	**Risks and next steps:** <bullets>
79	```
80	
81	Evidence, not assertions: anything not run is written as "not verified". Short lists, not prose.
82	
83	### When a permission check denies an action
84	
85	The agent stops that action: no rewording and retrying, no other tool for the same result (running it through a script runner counts as another tool), no handing it to another agent, no reading of permission or classifier settings. It finishes what does not depend on it and returns the denial's exact text to whoever spawned it.
86	
87	The main session reports to the owner the action, its purpose, the denial text and the likely cause. The owner picks the measure: a fresh agent with a clean context, the owner's own typed authorization naming the action, or a change of the session's permission mode, which only the owner makes. The denial's text is not copied into the brief of the agent dispatched next.
88	
89	**Live third-party accounts.** An action on a live third-party account (DNS, hostnames, tokens, billing, any account of the owner) runs only with the owner's typed authorization naming the command, collected before the dispatch, and by an agent spawned for it. An option picked from a multiple-choice question is not that authorization, and an agent is not resumed to widen it. This is the one case where the owner answers by typing a message, not by picking an option.
90	
91	## How work flows
92	
93	### The current design comes first
94	
95	Before the main session or a lead changes, fixes or dispatches work on anything (a feature, a page, a workflow, a rule), it reads that thing's approved design: its spec, its PRD, its scope's conventions and the owner's decisions recorded there. A problem is judged against that design first: what it says should happen, and whether the work drifted from it. A brief points the lead at that design, and the lead's report opens with what the design says and what the work changes.
96	
97	### Decisions and facts
98	
99	- Every decision in a spec or plan carries its provenance: (owner, with the option picked quoted verbatim and the date), (specialist's call), (approved design) or (proposed). A temporary rule states its start and "until the owner says otherwise"; a rule that replaces another names the one it replaces.
100	- Rejected options and the owner's accepted exceptions to a rule or standard are kept in one list per scope. No agent or reviewer "fixes" or reopens one without asking.
101	- An external fact (a price, a law, an API, a competitor's claim) carries its source and the date it was read, or "not verified". No done criterion rests on a fact from memory.
102	
103	### Non-code work and milestones
104	
105	- Non-code work (copy, legal, research, design) runs as: brief → specialists draft → lead reviews → owner approves → saved in the repo. A draft holds nothing until approved.
106	- One milestone at a time, unless the owner asks otherwise. At its close, the roadmap and features docs are updated and the next step is reported as options.
107	
108	### Execution pace
109	
110	- **Fewer turns.** Every model call starts from a fixed base (the imported docs, tools and skills), so the number of turns is the cost. Batch independent tool calls in one message. Resume a finished agent on the same thread instead of spawning anew, until rotation calls for a fresh one. An agent reports once, at the end of its task. No polling by repeated calls: wait with one command that ends on the condition.
111	- **Dispatch only what the task needs.** One task of one kind of work goes to one specialist. Splitting agents by area and kind of work does not mean more spawns: never spawn every specialist of an area "for coverage".
112	- **Stop rule.** After two rounds in which the measured number does not move toward the goal, the agent stops and reports options; no third round without the main session's OK.
113	
114	### Briefs
115	
116	- A brief points at a rule or a plan section by its line range; it never copies it. Copies drift. A brief to a specialist names the sections of the practices files it needs the same way.
117	- A brief never tells an agent to get around a tool's protection.
118	- A brief states the goal and what is ruled out, not a hypothesis: a brief that carries a hypothesis tends to come back confirmed.
119	- A brief passes an owner's choice with its intent and says what not to take literally. A question about a tone or a feeling names the effect in plain words, never a metaphor an agent could build literally.
120	- A brief gives a reviewer the owner's decisions as context, never as a list of what it must not look at.
121	- A brief ends with one line pointing at [Report format](#report-format-every-agent); that format replaces the report template of any other skill the agent runs.
122	{{- If CLAUDE.md has shell or file-reading rules: "A brief points at <that rule> and does not restate it."}}
123	
124	### Review cadence
125	
126	- **One owner each:** a lead owns exactly one area and a specialist does one kind of work. New work outside every agent's scope gets a new agent, not a wider one.
127	- **Adversarial review of domain work** runs in the area that owns it: a fresh instance of that area's lead, plus specialists who did not write the work. It never goes to the quality lead or reviewer.
128	- **Per task, by risk:** a read-only reviewer per task where production personal data, money, auth or a hard constraint is involved (test data in local or staging does not count). Low-risk tracks get one reviewer per group of tasks.
129	- A finding that is only wording is fixed directly, without a new review round.
130	- Reviewers and auditors are read-only agents (`disallowedTools: Edit, Write, NotebookEdit`).
131	- A verdict is given per requirement (met / not met / not verified), blocking gaps first with file, line and evidence, style marked optional. The reviewer reads a rule's whole file before judging by it, runs the gates itself, and checks by mutating the code that each rule is held by a test.
132	- A milestone review also reads across its tasks, for code that grew over several diffs. Reviewers only flag written rules, so a principle they must enforce is written once in the conventions or a practices file.
133	
134	### Parallel work
135	
136	- Agents run in parallel only when their scopes don't overlap.
137	- One writer at a time in the main checkout.
138	- An agent never deletes a file or folder it did not create in its task, git-ignored or untracked included; cleanup of shared state goes to its lead.
139	- An agent stops only the processes it started, by PID, never by name. Parallel checkouts get their own container, project and port names; nobody tears down a volume another checkout uses.
140	- A worktree is removed only when it has no uncommitted change and its commits are on the default branch; otherwise the main session decides.
141	- Claude Code runs at most {{20}} subagents at once and lets them nest {{three}} layers below the main session (its defaults; use the values the environment sets). Under a lead, a specialist is the second layer, so the helpers it spawns cannot spawn any.
142	- Worktrees: {{read-only work only}}. (default — tune)
143	
144	## Security posture (optional)
145	
146	{{pre-launch | in production}} (default — tune)
147	
148	{{pre-launch:}} Every owner step and every guard protects production, real users' data, money or a hard constraint — or the owner said yes to it knowing its cost in the owner's time per use. Staging and local credentials are created once, scoped, with no expiry or revocation ritual. Freeze and simplify: guards already built and working stay; rituals and new layers go. The simple option is the recommendation, with its accepted risk named in one line, written beside the rule it relaxes. Each spec, plan and runbook opens with this check, answered; a reviewer fails one without it.
149	{{in production: point at the project's security docs; don't restate them.}}
150	
151	## Owner-only actions
152	
153	Nobody but the owner does these. Agents prepare the exact steps and drafts; the owner acts. What only the owner's credentials can prove becomes a step in an owner runbook; agents prove the rest with fakes. A check that would need the owner to publish or send something becomes a synthetic request the agents make.
154	
155	- Creating or configuring third-party accounts, domains or services.
156	- Spending money.
157	- Filing, registering or signing anything.
158	- Publishing or sending anything public or to other people. No agent, the main session included, clicks, types or pastes into a field that publishes or sends (posts, comments, messages) in any account of the owner, even as a draft or to trigger a preview. A check that needs one is the owner's, on the owner's own device, or it is recorded as "not verified".
159	- Pushing or merging the default branch.
160	- Changing `.claude/` settings files (`.claude/settings*.json`) and permissions.
161	{{- Items from the owner's answer to "what must never happen without you".}}
162	
163	## Session hygiene
164	
165	- The main session keeps its context lean: reading and research go to agents; it keeps decisions and status.
166	- A rule the owner gives in conversation goes into this file or an agent file in the same session; memory files load only partly, and a fresh session starts without them.
167	- A rule a review or the owner adds cites its origin (date, and the review item or "owner"). A change to a rule or a constraint greps `.claude/agents/` for the old wording in the same commit.
168	- A rule or tooling fix is done only once it reaches the agents already running and its effect is measured. A rule that lives only in commands typed by hand drifts, so it goes into the script.
169	- Before `/clear` or `/compact`, the main session writes a handoff file with the goal, state, decisions and next steps.
170	- **Main-session rotation:** at a stop point, or when its transcript nears about {{5 MB}} of text (images excluded), the main session writes the handoff file and hands over to a **new top-level session**, never one nested under itself. The new session starts by reading the handoff and § Talking to the owner. Earlier main sessions are closed or archived.
171	- Before stopping a lead, or a process its children use (a container runtime, a dev server), the main session lists the lead's running children and stops them or waits for them. A stopped lead's queued messages still resume it.
172	- Merged worktrees and branches are cleaned up.
173	
174	## Periodic agent review
175	
176	{{off | on, weekly}} (default: off until the owner says yes; weekly when on — tune to the repo's commit rhythm)
177	
178	- It runs only on the owner's yes, in a separate session, conducted by {{the quality lead | a read-only reviewer the main session spawns for it}}.
179	- It covers the period's agent transcripts (summarized by a script, not read whole), commits, reports and denials.
180	- It delivers `docs/agent-reviews/YYYY-MM-DD.md` with fixed parts: the status of the previous review's items and of open incidents (held / partly / not held, with evidence); problems, highest impact first (agent, problem, evidence, proposed fix); cost by agent (runs, turns, tokens, active hours, from the transcripts by a script); what worked; not covered. Unused agent files are listed as removal candidates. After a change to the organization (agents split, merged or added), it compares cost per task (tokens, turns) before and after, and proposes a rollback when cost rose with no gain.
181	- **Incident records**, whether the review is on or off: a failure the owner calls serious gets a record in `docs/agent-reviews/incidents/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` the same day (timeline, causes, what changed, proposals). The next review dissects it first, with its measured cost.
182	- **A proposal closes only in a tracked file.** Each proposal of a review or an incident record is either applied in the docs or the agent files, with the owner's yes, or listed as declined. A note in a session's memory does not close it.
183	- Fixes land item by item, only with the owner's approval.

- The main session delegates every research, extraction, measurement and analysis from the first step; it briefs, decides and checks. Its effort is never lowered to save tokens.
- **Titles.** The Agent tool's `description` is the title the owner sees in the agent list. It starts with who the agent is, a pipe, then the task: `<Role> | <task>` (an ad-hoc member: `<Area> › <role> | <task>`). A title can't change later and a resumed agent keeps it, so a lead is named for its role, not its first task. Leads title their own spawns the same way.
- **Waiting for children.** A lead waits for every child it spawned to return, and hands back with their work committed. A child resumed with `SendMessage` runs in the background, even when its first run was in the foreground: a lead that resumes a child and needs its result does not end its turn, and waits with one blocking command that ends on the child's commit or report, never with repeated calls. If the lead is told to hand back while a child still runs, its report's status line is `BLOCKED: waiting for <child id>`, and the main session resumes the lead only after that child's notification.
- Before integrating a lead's work into a shared checkout, the main session runs `git status`; uncommitted work there means it resumes the lead to finish it.
- **Lead rotation:** a lead is replaced by a fresh one at each plan stop point, or when its transcript passes about {{5 MB}} of text (images excluded) or {{150}} model turns, whichever comes first. It is measured at each hand-back and before each `SendMessage` resume. (default — tune)

## Talking to the owner

- Only the main session talks to the owner. {{Point at the owner-contact rules already in CLAUDE.md, if any; then list here the owner working style items the owner turned on.}}
- Before asking, the main session checks whether the docs already answer the question; if so, it answers itself and cites the file.
- A prompt meant for an outside tool (a paid generator, an external service) is shown to the owner and approved before it is sent; a change of wording goes back to the owner.
- Subagents cannot ask the owner. When they need a decision they stop at a safe point and end their report with a questions block. The main session asks the owner, then resumes the agent with `SendMessage`, passing the answers verbatim.
- Before acting in a browser where the owner is signed in, the main session says in one line the site, the element and the text it will type, and acts on the owner's yes.

### Report format (every agent)

Headings in {{language}}. The first line is the status, so the spawner can act on it before reading the rest:

```
<DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED: <reason> | <reviewer verdict>>
## Report — <agent> — <task>
**Result:** <one line>
**Done:** <bullets>
**Evidence:** <commands run and what they returned, files>
**Files and commits:** <paths, commit hashes>
**Questions:**
1. <question> — context: <one line>; options: A (recommended) …, B …; blocking: yes/no; meanwhile: <what was done or skipped while waiting>
**Risks and next steps:** <bullets>
```

Evidence, not assertions: anything not run is written as "not verified". Short lists, not prose.

### When a permission check denies an action

The agent stops that action: no rewording and retrying, no other tool for the same result (running it through a script runner counts as another tool), no handing it to another agent, no reading of permission or classifier settings. It finishes what does not depend on it and returns the denial's exact text to whoever spawned it.

The main session reports to the owner the action, its purpose, the denial text and the likely cause. The owner picks the measure: a fresh agent with a clean context, the owner's own typed authorization naming the action, or a change of the session's permission mode, which only the owner makes. The denial's text is not copied into the brief of the agent dispatched next.

**Live third-party accounts.** An action on a live third-party account (DNS, hostnames, tokens, billing, any account of the owner) runs only with the owner's typed authorization naming the command, collected before the dispatch, and by an agent spawned for it. An option picked from a multiple-choice question is not that authorization, and an agent is not resumed to widen it. This is the one case where the owner answers by typing a message, not by picking an option.

## How work flows

### The current design comes first

Before the main session or a lead changes, fixes or dispatches work on anything (a feature, a page, a workflow, a rule), it reads that thing's approved design: its spec, its PRD, its scope's conventions and the owner's decisions recorded there. A problem is judged against that design first: what it says should happen, and whether the work drifted from it. A brief points the lead at that design, and the lead's report opens with what the design says and what the work changes.

### Decisions and facts

- Every decision in a spec or plan carries its provenance: (owner, with the option picked quoted verbatim and the date), (specialist's call), (approved design) or (proposed). A temporary rule states its start and "until the owner says otherwise"; a rule that replaces another names the one it replaces.
- Rejected options and the owner's accepted exceptions to a rule or standard are kept in one list per scope. No agent or reviewer "fixes" or reopens one without asking.
- An external fact (a price, a law, an API, a competitor's claim) carries its source and the date it was read, or "not verified". No done criterion rests on a fact from memory.

### Non-code work and milestones

- Non-code work (copy, legal, research, design) runs as: brief → specialists draft → lead reviews → owner approves → saved in the repo. A draft holds nothing until approved.
- One milestone at a time, unless the owner asks otherwise. At its close, the roadmap and features docs are updated and the next step is reported as options.

### Execution pace

- **Fewer turns.** Every model call starts from a fixed base (the imported docs, tools and skills), so the number of turns is the cost. Batch independent tool calls in one message. Resume a finished agent on the same thread instead of spawning anew, until rotation calls for a fresh one. An agent reports once, at the end of its task. No polling by repeated calls: wait with one command that ends on the condition.
- **Dispatch only what the task needs.** One task of one kind of work goes to one specialist. Splitting agents by area and kind of work does not mean more spawns: never spawn every specialist of an area "for coverage".
- **Stop rule.** After two rounds in which the measured number does not move toward the goal, the agent stops and reports options; no third round without the main session's OK.

### Briefs

- A brief points at a rule or a plan section by its line range; it never copies it. Copies drift. A brief to a specialist names the sections of the practices files it needs the same way.
- A brief never tells an agent to get around a tool's protection.
- A brief states the goal and what is ruled out, not a hypothesis: a brief that carries a hypothesis tends to come back confirmed.
- A brief passes an owner's choice with its intent and says what not to take literally. A question about a tone or a feeling names the effect in plain words, never a metaphor an agent could build literally.
- A brief gives a reviewer the owner's decisions as context, never as a list of what it must not look at.
- A brief ends with one line pointing at [Report format](#report-format-every-agent); that format replaces the report template of any other skill the agent runs.
{{- If CLAUDE.md has shell or file-reading rules: "A brief points at <that rule> and does not restate it."}}

### Review cadence

- **One owner each:** a lead owns exactly one area and a specialist does one kind of work. New work outside every agent's scope gets a new agent, not a wider one.
- **Adversarial review of domain work** runs in the area that owns it: a fresh instance of that area's lead, plus specialists who did not write the work. It never goes to the quality lead or reviewer.
- **Per task, by risk:** a read-only reviewer per task where production personal data, money, auth or a hard constraint is involved (test data in local or staging does not count). Low-risk tracks get one reviewer per group of tasks.
- A finding that is only wording is fixed directly, without a new review round.
- Reviewers and auditors are read-only agents (`disallowedTools: Edit, Write, NotebookEdit`).
- A verdict is given per requirement (met / not met / not verified), blocking gaps first with file, line and evidence, style marked optional. The reviewer reads a rule's whole file before judging by it, runs the gates itself, and checks by mutating the code that each rule is held by a test.
- A milestone review also reads across its tasks, for code that grew over several diffs. Reviewers only flag written rules, so a principle they must enforce is written once in the conventions or a practices file.

### Parallel work

- Agents run in parallel only when their scopes don't overlap.
- One writer at a time in the main checkout.
- An agent never deletes a file or folder it did not create in its task, git-ignored or untracked included; cleanup of shared state goes to its lead.
- An agent stops only the processes it started, by PID, never by name. Parallel checkouts get their own container, project and port names; nobody tears down a volume another checkout uses.
- A worktree is removed only when it has no uncommitted change and its commits are on the default branch; otherwise the main session decides.
- Claude Code runs at most {{20}} subagents at once and lets them nest {{three}} layers below the main session (its defaults; use the values the environment sets). Under a lead, a specialist is the second layer, so the helpers it spawns cannot spawn any.
- Worktrees: {{read-only work only}}. (default — tune)

## Security posture (optional)

{{pre-launch | in production}} (default — tune)

{{pre-launch:}} Every owner step and every guard protects production, real users' data, money or a hard constraint — or the owner said yes to it knowing its cost in the owner's time per use. Staging and local credentials are created once, scoped, with no expiry or revocation ritual. Freeze and simplify: guards already built and working stay; rituals and new layers go. The simple option is the recommendation, with its accepted risk named in one line, written beside the rule it relaxes. Each spec, plan and runbook opens with this check, answered; a reviewer fails one without it.
{{in production: point at the project's security docs; don't restate them.}}

## Owner-only actions

Nobody but the owner does these. Agents prepare the exact steps and drafts; the owner acts. What only the owner's credentials can prove becomes a step in an owner runbook; agents prove the rest with fakes. A check that would need the owner to publish or send something becomes a synthetic request the agents make.

- Creating or configuring third-party accounts, domains or services.
- Spending money.
- Filing, registering or signing anything.
- Publishing or sending anything public or to other people. No agent, the main session included, clicks, types or pastes into a field that publishes or sends (posts, comments, messages) in any account of the owner, even as a draft or to trigger a preview. A check that needs one is the owner's, on the owner's own device, or it is recorded as "not verified".
- Pushing or merging the default branch.
- Changing `.claude/` settings files (`.claude/settings*.json`) and permissions.
{{- Items from the owner's answer to "what must never happen without you".}}

## Session hygiene

- The main session keeps its context lean: reading and research go to agents; it keeps decisions and status.
- A rule the owner gives in conversation goes into this file or an agent file in the same session; memory files load only partly, and a fresh session starts without them.
- A rule a review or the owner adds cites its origin (date, and the review item or "owner"). A change to a rule or a constraint greps `.claude/agents/` for the old wording in the same commit.
- A rule or tooling fix is done only once it reaches the agents already running and its effect is measured. A rule that lives only in commands typed by hand drifts, so it goes into the script.
- Before `/clear` or `/compact`, the main session writes a handoff file with the goal, state, decisions and next steps.
- **Main-session rotation:** at a stop point, or when its transcript nears about {{5 MB}} of text (images excluded), the main session writes the handoff file and hands over to a **new top-level session**, never one nested under itself. The new session starts by reading the handoff and § Talking to the owner. Earlier main sessions are closed or archived.
- Before stopping a lead, or a process its children use (a container runtime, a dev server), the main session lists the lead's running children and stops them or waits for them. A stopped lead's queued messages still resume it.
- Merged worktrees and branches are cleaned up.

## Periodic agent review

{{off | on, weekly}} (default: off until the owner says yes; weekly when on — tune to the repo's commit rhythm)

- It runs only on the owner's yes, in a separate session, conducted by {{the quality lead | a read-only reviewer the main session spawns for it}}.
- It covers the period's agent transcripts (summarized by a script, not read whole), commits, reports and denials.
- It delivers `docs/agent-reviews/YYYY-MM-DD.md` with fixed parts: the status of the previous review's items and of open incidents (held / partly / not held, with evidence); problems, highest impact first (agent, problem, evidence, proposed fix); cost by agent (runs, turns, tokens, active hours, from the transcripts by a script); what worked; not covered. Unused agent files are listed as removal candidates. After a change to the organization (agents split, merged or added), it compares cost per task (tokens, turns) before and after, and proposes a rollback when cost rose with no gain.
- **Incident records**, whether the review is on or off: a failure the owner calls serious gets a record in `docs/agent-reviews/incidents/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` the same day (timeline, causes, what changed, proposals). The next review dissects it first, with its measured cost.
- **A proposal closes only in a tracked file.** Each proposal of a review or an incident record is either applied in the docs or the agent files, with the owner's yes, or listed as declined. A note in a session's memory does not close it.
- Fixes land item by item, only with the owner's approval.
